answer:
The right approach is to use Amazon SNS FIFO topics to distribute the events to the necessary services. SNS FIFO topics guarantee message ordering and exactly-once delivery, addressing the requirement for ordered, concurrent event delivery to multiple targets. SNS standard topics (Publish events to an Amazon SNS standard topic for concurrent processing) do not ensure message ordering or eliminate duplicate deliveries. Amazon EventBridge event buses support event routing but do not natively guarantee strict ordering of events as they are processed by various targets. Amazon SQS FIFO queues enforce ordering but require consumers to poll separately, which doesn't achieve concurrent delivery to multiple services since each queue is for a single set of consumers or requires complex orchestration. SNS FIFO topics are tailor-made for this use case, ensuring every subscribed service receives and processes events in the required sequence.

Tip: Use SNS FIFO topics anytime you need fan-out and ordering guarantees together. Remember that FIFO SQS is ideal for strict ordered single-group processing, not fan-out to many microservices.

Automated backups in Amazon RDS support point-in-time recovery, permitting you to restore your database to any specific time within your backup retention window, up to the previous 35 days. The following explains why the other options are incorrect:

  • Read replicas are intended primarily for scaling read traffic and some disaster recovery scenarios. They do not enable restoring the database to an exact moment within the backup window.

Tip: Enable automated backups with an appropriate retention period to maximize your ability to recover from accidental data modifications. Always test your recovery procedures periodically to ensure compliance with business continuity requirements.

answer:
The Set up a NAT gateway in a public subnet and update the route tables for each private subnet to direct default traffic to this NAT gateway. option is correct. A NAT gateway is a fully managed AWS service that enables instances in private subnets to initiate outbound connections to the internet while blocking unsolicited inbound traffic. Placing the NAT gateway in a public subnet ensures it has a public IP address and internet access. Route tables in private subnets must point their default route (0.0.0.0/0) to this NAT gateway for internet-bound requests. This approach is highly available across multiple Availability Zones (if configured per AZ), scalable, and requires minimal operational management from the user, aligning with the company's need for a managed solution with low maintenance.

The other options do not meet AWS recommended best practices or are incorrect for the following reasons:

  • Deploy a NAT instance within a private subnet and configure each private subnet's route table to use this NAT instance as the default route. — This is incorrect because NAT instances and gateways must reside in a public subnet to provide internet connectivity to private subnet resources. Placing the NAT instance in a private subnet prevents the required internet access.
  • Launch a NAT gateway inside a private subnet and point the default route of the private subnets to this NAT gateway. — Incorrect for similar reasons. A NAT gateway in a private subnet will not function correctly because it won’t have a public IP and cannot route traffic out to the internet.
  • Provision a NAT instance in a public subnet and configure the private subnets' route tables to send all internet-bound traffic via this NAT instance. — While NAT instances work when placed in public subnets, NAT gateways are the managed, highly available, scalable solution AWS recommends. NAT instances require more operational work (patching, scaling, failover setup), which the question says should be minimized.

Tip: Always choose NAT gateways over NAT instances unless cost or legacy constraints dictate otherwise, because NAT gateways are fully managed, auto-scaled, and require minimal maintenance.

  • Utilize Amazon Route 53 for distributing client requests and Aurora Serverless for the backing data store: Route 53 can help with DNS-based routing but doesn't distribute UDP traffic to resources in the required manner, and Aurora Serverless is still a relational database, not tailored for non-relational, highly dynamic game metadata.

The best option is to use Amazon ElastiCache to temporarily store frequently accessed data. ElastiCache acts as an in-memory datastore or cache, letting frequently used queries be served quickly without repeatedly hitting the RDS database. This significantly minimizes response times and offloads read pressure from your primary database.

Why the other options are suboptimal or incorrect:

  • Deploy Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to transmit database requests to RDS: Kinesis Data Firehose is designed for real-time streaming data delivery, not for accelerating or caching database queries. It doesn't address repeated data retrieval nor does it reduce database load.
  • Set up Amazon SNS to retain incoming database queries: Amazon SNS is a notification and messaging service, not a caching or persistence solution for database calls. It cannot provide faster data retrieval as required here.
  • Create a read replica of the RDS MySQL database to cache repeated queries: While an RDS read replica helps distribute read queries, it’s not specifically a cache and won’t offer the ultra-low latencies or deduplication for repeated identical queries that a caching layer like ElastiCache can provide.

Tip: Use a caching solution such as ElastiCache when workloads involve repeated fetching of the same data. This can greatly improve scalability and user experience by easing the burden on your relational databases.

Tip: Always align your data retention policies in streaming services with your downstream processing schedules to avoid unintentional data loss.

answer:
Apply an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition the bucket's objects to S3 Intelligent-Tiering is the best choice when access patterns are unknown and you want to minimize operational effort. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between frequent and infrequent access tiers as access patterns change, optimizing storage costs without requiring continuous manual evaluation or policy changes. It doesn't require prior knowledge of how often data is accessed, making it ideal for unpredictable or changing data access.

The other answers are less effective:

  • Rely on S3 storage class analysis to manually assess and relocate each object to its optimal storage class: This method requires constant manual assessment and movement of objects based on report findings, which is resource-intensive and operationally inefficient, especially for vast datasets with unknown usage patterns. It doesn't automate cost optimization.
  • Establish a Lifecycle rule to shift objects to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval storage class: While Glacier Instant Retrieval is low-cost, it is designed for archiving data that is rarely accessed. Moving all data there could lead to higher retrieval costs and latency if data is accessed frequently, and is not suitable when patterns are unknown.
  • Set a Lifecycle rule so that all objects transition to S3 One Zone-IA: One Zone-IA stores data in a single Availability Zone, reducing cost but increasing risk if a zone fails. It is best for non-critical, infrequently accessed data. Without understanding which data qualifies, this is risky and not optimal.

Tip: Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering for datasets with changing or unknown access patterns and when you need cost savings with minimal operational overhead. Lifecycle rules can automate transitions to this storage class, further improving efficiency.

This approach allows team members from the development account to assume the designated IAM role in the production account, thereby receiving only the necessary permissions to access the S3 bucket. This method follows the principle of least privilege and leverages cross-account role assumption, a best practice recommended by AWS for secure resource sharing between accounts.

Tip: Always use cross-account IAM roles with trust policies for secure sharing between AWS accounts, and never lower bucket-level security controls like Block Public Access unless public sharing is absolutely necessary and justified.

The "Deploy an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster and send all of your read queries to the reader endpoint" option is the best fit for this scenario. RDS Multi-AZ DB clusters for PostgreSQL provide automatic failover support typically under 40 seconds, meeting the high availability and automatic failover requirements. The cluster deployment also offers a dedicated reader endpoint that efficiently load-balances read queries across read-only instances, so you can offload read workloads from the primary DB instance and help reduce costs since you avoid provisioning extra replicas unnecessarily.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • "Set up an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance and direct your read operations to the standby instance within the Multi-AZ configuration." — In Multi-AZ instance deployments, the standby instance is only for failover and does not serve read traffic; it cannot be used to offload reads.
  • "Configure an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, add a read replica, and send your read queries to this replica." — While read replicas can be used for read scaling, this solution uses an RDS instance deployment, not a DB cluster. The failover time is usually longer, and it does not address clustering or cost effectiveness as fully as the DB cluster model does.
  • "Set up an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster with two dedicated read replicas and direct read requests to those replicas." — While possible, creating additional dedicated read replicas increases complexity and costs unnecessarily, since the cluster's built-in reader endpoint can distribute reads among already-provisioned reader nodes efficiently.

Tip: For RDS for PostgreSQL workloads that require high availability, low failover downtime, and easy read scaling, Multi-AZ DB clusters with reader endpoints are ideal. Multi-AZ instances serve only as failover targets and do not help scale read workloads.

answer:
"Route API requests into an Amazon SQS queue. Deploy the ML models as services on Amazon ECS that consume from the queue. Utilize AWS Auto Scaling for ECS to scale both the cluster and service instances according to the SQS queue length." is the best option here.

This approach works especially well because ECS services can efficiently handle large workloads that require significant memory (such as loading 1 GB of model data from S3 at startup). By using an Amazon SQS queue, the system naturally supports asynchronous processing and workload decoupling, while Auto Scaling enables rapid adjustment to spikes or lulls in traffic—perfect for unpredictable workloads. ECS tasks can persist with loaded model data, reducing cold start latency for heavy models.

"Send incoming API requests to a Network Load Balancer (NLB), with each ML model built as an AWS Lambda function triggered directly by the NLB." is not feasible because NLB cannot directly trigger Lambda functions; Lambda is typically integrated with Application Load Balancer (ALB), not NLB. Also, running large models (1 GB cold start) on AWS Lambda is not efficient or scalable, as Lambda is best suited for lightweight, stateless, short-lived processes.

"Direct all requests from the API to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Set up Amazon ECS services for the ML models, where they retrieve work from an SQS queue, and apply AWS App Mesh to automatically scale ECS instances in response to the queue depth." is unnecessarily complex. Routing work through an ALB is typically used for synchronous interactions, but in this scenario the API and workload processing are decoupled. Bringing AWS App Mesh adds advanced service mesh features but is not required just for scaling based on SQS backlog.

"Forward API requests into an Amazon SQS queue. Deploy ML models as AWS Lambda functions that process SQS events, and use AWS Auto Scaling to add Lambda vCPUs as queue size grows." is not appropriate since Lambda's memory and duration limits make it impractical to load 1 GB models and perform resource-intensive processing. Also, Lambda has fixed resource allocation; you can't directly scale vCPUs independently of allocated memory.

Tips: For long-running, resource-intensive, or large memory workloads, containers (ECS/EKS) are superior to Lambda. Queue-based architectures with decoupled consumers scale flexibly to meet workload bursts. Understand how AWS scaling and integration patterns impact service design.

Role and Group are the only IAM principal types that support attachment of identity-based policies directly. These policies define what actions principals can perform within AWS.

Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) resource and Amazon EC2 resource are services/resources, not IAM identities, and therefore cannot have identity-based policies directly assigned to them. Instead, permissions for these resources are managed either through IAM roles (which are then associated for resource access) or resource-based policies.

Organization refers to AWS Organizations, which does not support direct attachment of IAM identity-based policies. Service control policies (SCPs) are used at the organization level for permission boundaries.

Tip: When dealing with identity-based policies in AWS, remember they are assigned to IAM users, groups, or roles—not to specific AWS service resources or your entire AWS organization.

Utilize AWS DataSync to seamlessly move the existing files to Amazon S3, and enable AWS CloudTrail to log data events is the correct answer. AWS DataSync is optimized for securely and efficiently migrating large amounts of on-premises data to Amazon S3, making it a strong choice for frequent or bulk data transfer scenarios, especially with changing data. By enabling AWS CloudTrail to log data events, the company can track all access and modification activities at the object-level in S3, which is required for audit and compliance purposes in the healthcare industry.

Option "Use AWS Snowcone to transfer the existing data to Amazon S3 and configure AWS CloudTrail to record management events." is not appropriate for this case. Option "Set up Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration for rapid data migration to Amazon S3, and turn on CloudTrail for data event logging." is partially correct because S3 Transfer Acceleration is designed for accelerating uploads from geographically dispersed clients via optimized network paths. However, it is not designed for large-scale migrations or recurring sync operations—DataSync is more robust for this use case.

Option "Leverage AWS Storage Gateway to migrate files to Amazon S3 while using AWS CloudTrail to record management events." falls short since AWS Storage Gateway is mainly for hybrid cloud storage scenarios, and management event logging does not provide the detailed object-level access logs that data events in CloudTrail deliver.

Tip: For regulatory audit requirements, always log S3 data events in CloudTrail, not just management events. And for one-off or ongoing transfers of changing datasets from on-premises to S3, DataSync is the service purpose-built for migration and sync tasks. Understanding the difference between management and data events in CloudTrail, and choosing the right migration service for your scenario, is vital for AWS exam success.

The MOST secure way for a Lambda function to access a DynamoDB table is to use an IAM role configured as the execution role for the Lambda function, granting necessary permissions. The correct option is "Configure an IAM role with AWS Lambda as a trusted service, attach permissions for DynamoDB table read and write, and assign this role as the Lambda execution role." This method leverages temporary credentials managed by AWS and ensures least-privilege, reducing credential exposure risks.

"Set up an IAM user with programmatic access rights for the Lambda function, grant the user a policy for DynamoDB table read and write, and store the user's access keys as Lambda environment variables. Prevent other users from accessing the Lambda configuration." is less secure because storing long-term credentials within Lambda environment variables increases the risk of accidental leakage or misuse.

"Define an IAM user with programmatic access for the Lambda function, attach a read and write DynamoDB policy, save the access keys as secure parameters in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, and update the Lambda code to pull these parameters before accessing DynamoDB." is still insecure as it relies on long-lived credentials, even if stored as secure strings. This does not follow AWS best practices for authentication within services.

"Establish an IAM role with DynamoDB as a trusted service, attach a policy granting Lambda read and write access, and modify the Lambda code to use this role as its execution role." is incorrect, as the trust policy should identify Lambda as the trusted principal, not DynamoDB. This would not allow Lambda to assume the role and obtain credentials.

Tip: Always follow the principle of least privilege and use short-lived, automatically rotated credentials (such as those provided by execution roles) in serverless AWS environments. Avoid using static access keys wherever possible.

The correct answer is: Group members can stop and terminate instances only in the us-east-1 Region with MFA, and may perform any other EC2 actions in us-east-1.

This is because the Deny statement explicitly blocks ec2:StopInstances and ec2:TerminateInstances in us-east-1 unless MFA has been used. For all other EC2 actions in us-east-1, the Allow applies freely (no MFA is required). The scope of these permissions does not extend to other regions for stopping/terminating, and the only requirement for MFA is for these two actions in us-east-1.

Let's review why the other options are wrong:

  • Unless authenticated with multi-factor authentication (MFA), group members are denied all Amazon EC2 actions in us-east-1. – This is too broad; the Deny is specifically limited to stop/terminate actions, not all EC2 actions.
  • Members are allowed to stop and terminate Amazon EC2 instances in any AWS Region if they use MFA, but can perform any other EC2 action anywhere. – The permission only applies to the us-east-1 region for stop/terminate, not all regions.
  • All EC2 actions in the us-east-1 Region are permitted for group members, and no statements after the Allow permission apply. – This ignores how explicit Deny statements in IAM always override Allow statements, so the order of statements does matter.

Tip: Remember that in IAM, Deny statements have higher precedence than Allow. Also, the condition (like MFA authentication) in the Deny will make exceptions only for specified permissions, not all permissions.

The most cost-effective and operationally sound combination is to:

  1. Set up S3 Lifecycle rules to move .csv files from the S3 Standard storage class to S3 Glacier a day after upload, and automatically delete image files after 30 days. Storing .csv files in S3 Glacier minimizes ongoing costs because the files are rarely accessed and their retrieval can be planned in advance, fitting Glacier's use case and cost advantages. Automatically expiring image files after 30 days matches their disposable nature, ensuring storage efficiency.
  2. Use an AWS Lambda function, triggered by each .csv upload, to convert .csv data into images and store them in the S3 bucket. Lambda enables immediate, event-driven conversions without the need for ongoing server maintenance. It scales automatically and is highly cost-effective for sporadic workloads related to file uploads.

'Provision an EC2 Spot Instance that downloads .csv files hourly, generates image files, and puts them back into the S3 bucket' is inefficient due to unnecessary complexity and ongoing costs associated with running and maintaining an EC2 instance for what can be an event-driven task. 'Establish S3 Lifecycle rules to move .csv files from S3 Standard to S3 One Zone-IA after one day, and remove image files after they're 30 days old' is suboptimal because One Zone-IA is not as cost-efficient as S3 Glacier for seldom-accessed files and offers lower durability. 'Create S3 Lifecycle rules to send .csv files to S3 Standard-IA one day post-upload while putting image files in Reduced Redundancy Storage' is outdated and not recommended, as Reduced Redundancy Storage is designed for non-critical data and is being phased out in favor of other storage classes with better durability and pricing and wouldn't offer cost benefits for image files that must be readily available for a month.

Tips: For rarely accessed data where retrieval can be planned, S3 Glacier is the most economical choice. Lambda functions reduce complexity and cost for file-based processing in AWS. Use lifecycle policies to automate management and deletion of temporary files for cost savings.

The Amazon ElastiCache for Redis solution is the best choice for this scenario. Redis supports advanced data structures such as sorted sets, which are ideal for maintaining a real-time top-10 scoreboard with millions of rapid updates. It also offers persistence options that help preserve the scores even if the cluster is restarted or if the game is paused and resumed by users. Redis is designed for low-latency reads and writes, enabling the web application to retrieve the most current scoreboard quickly.

The other options are less appropriate:

  • Place an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the web application to cache and serve the scoreboard for a portion of the application.: CloudFront is primarily for caching static content at edge locations and doesn't support the high frequency of changes required for near-real-time scoreboards.
  • Deploy Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached to temporarily cache player scores for the web application display.: While Memcached can cache data, it doesn't support advanced data structures needed to efficiently manage and compute a top-10 scoreboard, nor does it offer data persistence, so scores could be lost if the cache is restarted.
  • Add a read replica to the Amazon RDS for MySQL database to execute queries for scoreboard computation and to handle read requests from the web application.: While read replicas can help scale read requests, computing a real-time scoreboard with frequent updates can still introduce latency and add significant load to the database, which is not optimal for performance or scalability.

Tip: Use Redis sorted sets for leaderboards or top-N rankings where both performance and durability are critical, and always consider persistence when temporary data loss is unacceptable.

The best option is to configure Amazon Route 53 health checks for every Region and use an active-active failover setup for routing requests. Route 53 allows you to direct traffic based on the health of your endpoints and can evenly distribute user requests across multiple regional endpoints for high availability. If one Region becomes unreachable, Route 53 automatically diverts traffic to healthy endpoints in other Regions, ensuring continuous service.

"Set up a distribution in Amazon CloudFront, specifying an origin for each Region and using CloudFront health checks to manage regional traffic routing.": While CloudFront improves latency and delivers content from edge locations, it doesn't natively understand how to route based on overall API health per Region the way Route 53 does. CloudFront health checks are more oriented toward checking the origin's health but do not provide global, multi-Region failover for API endpoints.

"Deploy an Application Load Balancer in the primary Region and configure target groups to direct traffic to API Gateway endpoints in all Regions.": Application Load Balancers are regional resources and do not support cross-Region distribution or failover for API Gateway endpoints. They're suitable within a single Region, not across multiple Regions.

"Create a transit gateway, connect it to the API Gateway endpoints across all Regions, and set up routing tables to distribute incoming requests.": Transit gateways are used for VPC-to-VPC connectivity within and between Regions but are not designed for global DNS-based traffic routing to API endpoints.

Pro Tip: For global applications requiring failover across Regions, Route 53 DNS-based routing with health checks provides the required resiliency and control for both active-active and active-passive architectures.

  • Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution endpoint.   • Provision an Amazon CloudFront distribution endpoint. Place a Network Load Balancer (NLB) behind the CDN, listening for TCP and UDP traffic, and register the servers managed by the Auto Scaling group to the NLB. Tip: For low latency, global reach, and support for both TCP and UDP, consider Global Accelerator. NLBs work with both TCP and UDP, whereas ALBs are HTTP/HTTPS only. CloudFront is not suitable for non-HTTP/HTTPS traffic or real-time game traffic like this scenario.

The option that leverages Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) with EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer provides the most reliable and scalable way to ensure orders are written to the database quickly and efficiently. By placing orders onto an SQS queue, the application decouples order ingestion from processing, which allows for greater resilience and improved throughput, especially during spikes in traffic. EC2 Auto Scaling lets the processing capacity dynamically adjust as the queue depth grows, so the system can handle bursts in admissions without losing records.

Let’s examine why the other choices are less suitable:

  • Direct incoming orders to Amazon SNS and subscribe the database endpoint to the SNS topic. Use an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer to process orders from SNS. — SNS is best for pub/sub or fan-out messaging patterns, but it doesn't queue messages for retries or delayed processing. Databases aren't designed to be SNS subscribers, and there is a risk of data loss if the processing target is unresponsive.
  • Scale up the Amazon EC2 instance size during high-demand periods. Publish orders to Amazon SNS and subscribe the database endpoint to the topic. — Resizing the instance only adds limited, vertical scalability. This does not address message queuing or decoupling, and again, SNS lacks built-in queuing which makes this solution unreliable for order processing during surges.
  • When the EC2 instance reaches high CPU usage, enqueue incoming orders into Amazon SQS. Use a scheduled scaling policy on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group, fronted by an Application Load Balancer, to process orders from the queue to the database. — Delaying queuing until a CPU threshold is hit can result in lost orders and unnecessary latency. Scheduled scaling might not scale quickly or responsively enough to cope with sudden traffic spikes, reducing reliability.

Tips: Use SQS for critical, bursty workloads needing durable queuing and scalable, decoupled processing. Always prefer SQS over SNS for asynchronous task processing. Auto Scaling groups offer the flexibility to match processing capacity to workload in real time.

The write-through caching approach guarantees that any modifications in the database are immediately reflected in the cache. As soon as a customer adds or modifies data in the database, the cache is updated accordingly. This ensures strong consistency—what's in the cache always mirrors the underlying database content.

  • Configure a lazy loading cache strategy. - Lazy loading only populates the cache when a read request occurs for missing data; it is possible for the cache to have outdated data if the database is modified outside of the cache's read flow, leading to potential inconsistencies.
  • Introduce a cache with a time-to-live (TTL) policy. - A TTL setting causes items to expire after a set duration, but does not guarantee that the cache will always be in sync with the database—there can still be a window in which the data is stale.
  • Use the AWS AppConfig caching method. - AWS AppConfig is a service for deploying application configuration, not for application data caching; it is irrelevant to the use case described.

Tip: For strict consistency between cache and database, write-through (or write-around) caching is a best practice as it tightly couples cache updates to database changes.

The best solution is to use an S3 Lifecycle configuration that deletes expired object versions while keeping only the most recent two versions. This leverages built-in S3 capabilities, requires minimal ongoing attention, and operates automatically at scale. The lifecycle policies can be defined to transition or remove past versions based on object age or count, which directly addresses the cost issue by automatically purging extra versions.

Set up an AWS Lambda function to periodically identify older object versions and delete all except the two most recent ones introduces more operational overhead since you would need to write, schedule, and maintain code, increasing complexity compared to the native lifecycle option.

Turn off versioning for the S3 bucket and manually keep the latest two versions of each object is risky and can lead to accidental data loss, and versioning cannot be simply turned off to keep prior versions—when versioning is suspended, all versions remain but no new versions are created; also, S3 does not natively delete older versions when versioning stops.

Utilize S3 Batch Operations to remove outdated versions, retaining just the newest two per object is suited for one-off or occasional bulk cleanup, not for continuous ongoing management, so it results in higher overhead in the long run.

Tips: Leverage native AWS features wherever possible for low maintenance and better reliability, especially for tasks like object lifecycle management in S3.

The correct choices are Schedule DataSync tasks to transfer data directly from on-premises servers to FSx for Windows File Server by deploying AWS DataSync agents onsite and Acquire an AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device, connect it to the local network, transfer the files using the AWS CLI, return the device to AWS so the data is imported into S3, and then use DataSync to move the files into FSx for Windows File Server. Both of these solutions are capable of handling large-scale migration while preserving NTFS file permissions and attributes, which is critical for Windows file shares.

Why are these two options correct?

  • Deploying AWS DataSync agents onsite allows for direct, secure migration of files from your on-premises servers to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server with permission fidelity. DataSync is specifically engineered to preserve NTFS attributes throughout the transfer process.
  • Using a Snowball Edge device as an intermediary can be useful for substantial datasets that might exceed your available internet bandwidth. After the data is loaded onto Snowball Edge and returned to AWS, DataSync orchestrates further migration into FSx, assuring that file system metadata, including permissions, is retained.

Why are the other choices incorrect?
  • Utilize the AWS CLI to copy file shares from the on-premises servers into Amazon S3, and then configure AWS DataSync jobs to migrate the data into FSx for Windows File Server. — This approach will not reliably maintain NTFS permissions because the AWS CLI does not retain file-level metadata such as ACLs when copying files to S3.
  • Detach drives from each Windows file server, send the hardware to AWS for S3 data ingestion, followed by scheduling DataSync operations that copy the data to FSx for Windows File Server. — This process is not practical and introduces risk. Physical drive removal and shipment to AWS via the Import service do not guarantee preservation of Windows file permissions and extend migration timelines.
  • Order an AWS Snowcone device, link it to the on-premises network, run AWS DataSync agents on the device, and plan DataSync tasks to migrate data into FSx for Windows File Server. — AWS Snowcone does not natively support the scale and storage requirements typical of full-scale Windows file server migrations, and its integration with FSx migrations is limited compared to Snowball Edge.

Tips: Prefer DataSync for permission-aware transfers and only use AWS physical transfer devices (such as Snowball Edge) for large data sets or where network bandwidth is limited. Always verify that tools/processes involved in migration support NTFS ACL preservation.

The best solutions to enhance both the performance and resilience of the website involve making the storage and compute layers more scalable and reliable.

  • Copy the website images to an Amazon EFS file system and mount EFS to all relevant EC2 instances. EFS provides a shared, scalable file system that multiple EC2 instances can mount concurrently, overcoming single-node bottlenecks and failures. It ensures images are not stored on a single instance’s EBS volume, allowing for improved availability and seamless scaling across instances.
  • Launch new EC2 instances using an AMI created from the current instance, place them behind an Application Load Balancer within an Auto Scaling group (minimum two instances), and set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the website. This combination introduces high availability by removing the single EC2 instance failure point, allows for easy scaling based on demand, and leverages CloudFront’s caching to enhance performance and decrease load times for global users.

Here’s why the other choices are not ideal:

  • Use an NFS share provided by the main EC2 instance… keeps the architecture dependent on a single EC2 instance for image storage, introducing a potential single point of failure and limiting scalability.
  • Migrate the website images into an S3 bucket and mount this bucket on each EC2 instance. While S3 is excellent for storing static assets, 'mounting' S3 buckets on EC2 is not natively supported for direct file system operations; using EFS is the preferred shared file system for this use case.
  • Provision new EC2 instances from an AMI… and configure AWS Global Accelerator… While Global Accelerator improves global edge routing and availability, it does not address the need for a scalable, concurrent solution for shared image storage between EC2 instances, nor offer the caching benefits of CloudFront.

Tip: Use Amazon EFS for file sharing across EC2 instances, and always consider CloudFront for accelerating content delivery and reducing origin load. When scaling out web architectures, removing reliance on single-instance resources ensures resilience and improved uptime.

The correct solution is for customers to create an IAM role with a trust policy that allows the company’s account to assume it, and grants the necessary read-only permissions on EC2 and CloudWatch. This method is highly secure because it:

  • Uses cross-account IAM roles, which is an AWS best practice for delegating access between accounts.
  • Allows for granular permission control and auditing.
  • No long-term credentials are stored or shared.

Other options present security or operational drawbacks:

  • Configure a serverless API as a token vending machine to distribute temporary AWS credentials that have read-only EC2 and CloudWatch privileges.
    This introduces significant complexity and operational overhead while duplicating what AWS native cross-account roles do securely and natively.
  • Instruct customers to provision an IAM user with read-only EC2 and CloudWatch access, then securely store those credentials in a secret manager solution.
    This requires the customer to hand over long-term access keys, increasing exposure and violating least privilege and credential management best practices.
  • Have customers create an Amazon Cognito user assigned with read-only EC2 and CloudWatch role, and store the Cognito credentials securely.
    Amazon Cognito is intended for managing authentication of end users for applications—not for cross-account AWS resource access between companies.

Tip: Always use cross-account roles and trust policies when building SaaS or service integrations that require delegated AWS resource access, and never use hard-coded credentials.

Update the network ACLs associated with the web tier subnets to add inbound deny entries for the offending IP addresses. This is the best immediate action: Network ACLs (NACLs) are stateless firewall rules that operate at the subnet level, allowing you to explicitly deny traffic from specified sources. By updating the NACL for public web subnets, you ensure that the malicious requests are dropped before they even reach your instances or security groups, providing a quick and scalable block.

Why not the other options?

"Change the inbound security group of the web-facing tier to include deny rules specifically blocking the problematic IP addresses." Security groups do not support explicit deny rules—only allow rules—so this won't work for blocking unwanted addresses.

"Apply deny rules in the inbound security group of the application tier to reject traffic from the abusive IP addresses." Similar to the above, security groups can't explicitly deny, and the application layer is in private subnets, which means traffic from the ALB would be allowed through anyway.

"Configure the network ACLs on the application tier subnets to block inbound requests from the identified IP addresses." Blocking at the application tier's NACL only covers the private layer, but since the attack targets the web ALB in the public subnets, this won’t stop the malicious traffic before stressing the public web subnet resources.

Tip: Use NACLs for rapid subnet-level blocking when you need explicit deny, especially for immediate remediation of abusive sources. For long-term solutions, consider AWS WAF for advanced filtering.

  • Launch additional Aurora PostgreSQL read replicas to support the load during failover events: Read replicas only assist with read workloads and do not serve write traffic.   • Provision a secondary Aurora PostgreSQL cluster in the same AWS Region and reconfigure your application to switch endpoints during failover: This approach introduces significant operational burden.   • Implement an Amazon ElastiCache Memcached cluster to alleviate the database workload during failover windows: While adding caching can reduce database load, it does not address the application's ability to write to the database or seamlessly handle failover. ElastiCache does not mitigate writer instance failover downtime for OLTP applications.

Tip: RDS Proxy is purpose-built to manage failovers transparently to client applications, maintain fewer dropped connections, and minimize recovery time, making it the best-fit, low-effort solution in this scenario.

Also, read replicas can be used for reporting, but this still leaves a single point of failure and does not offer automatic failover.
  • Launch an Amazon Aurora cluster in Multi-AZ with Amazon RDS and divert reporting operations to Aurora reader replicas: Although Aurora is designed for high scalability and high availability, the question specifically refers to Oracle, not Aurora. This makes the option inapplicable when an Oracle database is required.

Additionally, using AWS DMS for ongoing replication can be more complex to manage and does not provide as seamless a failover or offload solution as built-in Multi-AZ clusters with read endpoints.

Tip: For Amazon RDS (including Oracle), Multi-AZ cluster deployments support one or more reader nodes, which can be used for read-scale workloads such as reporting. Leveraging built-in high availability with reader endpoints is both operationally efficient and robust.

The most reliable approach is to implement a canary deployment stage for the API Gateway service. Deploy the newest API code and direct a chosen percentage of incoming requests to the canary stage. Once verified, elevate the canary version to production status. This process enables gradual exposure of the new API version and provides a safety net, allowing verification with minimal customer impact and reducing the likelihood of data loss. Traffic can be incrementally shifted as confidence in the new version increases.

As for the other choices:

  • Deploy the updated API version to a new API Gateway endpoint, then configure a custom domain for this new API. Update the Route 53 alias record to point to the custom domain of the newer API Gateway endpoint. – This option risks causing disruptions since updating the DNS alias can lead to propagation delays and possible data loss during the switch.
  • Upload the latest API version using an OpenAPI JSON file in import-to-update mode with the overwrite option for the API Gateway endpoint. Deploy the overwritten API to production. – Using overwrite in import-to-update mode is risky, as it might remove existing resources and result in outage or loss of data for ongoing connections.
  • Publish a new API Gateway endpoint using an OpenAPI YAML definition, and then perform a merge-based import-to-update operation into the existing API Gateway. Roll out the new API version directly to production. – While safer than overwrite, merge mode still carries risk as changes are applied immediately, and there is minimal opportunity for staged testing or rollback with real user traffic.

Tip: Canary deployments are recommended for environments requiring high availability and zero-downtime releases, as they promote smooth transitions and allow quick rollback in case of unforeseen issues.

This solution is highly resilient, requires minimal infrastructure, and aligns best with the company's goal of minimizing changes and ongoing overhead.

  • Enable multivalue answer routing in Route 53. Create a health check, and serve traffic to the main site if it passes, or to an S3 error page if the check does not pass. – Multivalue answer routing can perform health checks, but it's intended to provide multiple healthy endpoints to clients, not for true failover; it doesn't guarantee all users will reach the error page during a failure scenario.

The optimal choice is Configure an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) instance and mount it on every EC2 instance. Amazon EFS is designed for scalable, shared file storage that supports concurrent access from multiple EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. It enables fast and parallel read and write operations, and it fully supports hierarchical directory structures that applications rely on.

Here's why the alternatives are not suitable:

Provision an Amazon S3 bucket and allow all EC2 instances within the VPC to access it. – Amazon S3 is object storage, not a POSIX-compliant file system. It does not provide hierarchical directory structures or the ability for multiple EC2 instances to perform high-speed concurrent read/write operations typical of shared file systems.

Set up individual file systems on Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) volumes, attaching a separate volume to each EC2 instance and synchronizing the data between all volumes. – EBS volumes are designed for single-instance attachment (except for some specific multi-attach scenarios with limitations) and synchronizing file systems manually across instances is complex, inefficient, and prone to data inconsistencies.

Create a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) Amazon EBS volume with a file system, then attach the same EBS volume to multiple EC2 instances for shared file access. – Although newer EBS volumes support multi-attach for certain use cases, multi-attach is primarily intended for clustered applications and databases that handle their own data consistency. Traditional file systems are not safe to use with multi-attach, as this can cause data corruption.

Tip: When applications need a shared file system accessible by multiple EC2 instances across Availability Zones, always consider Amazon EFS for its scalability, concurrency, and NFS compatibility.

SnapStart is specifically designed for Java-based AWS Lambda functions (Java 11+) and works by taking a snapshot of the Lambda execution environment after initialization. Increase the Lambda function's memory allocation can sometimes help marginally with cold starts, but it is not designed to specifically address startup latency or reduce cold starts in a predictable or cost-effective way; it may also increase cost for little effect.

Lengthen the Lambda function execution timeout does not affect initialization latency or cold start behavior; it only allows functions to run longer. This setting does not address the latency or scaling concerns in this scenario.

The correct answer is Deploy EC2 On-Demand Instances with activated hibernation and configure Auto Scaling warm pools to optimize initialization during future testing. Hibernation allows an instance to save its in-memory state to disk so that, when restarted, the system memory is quickly restored to its pre-shutdown state. Using Auto Scaling warm pools enables you to keep pre-initialized instances ready, which minimizes both boot and application initialization time, greatly improving startup performance during high-demand or testing.

Here's why the other options are less suitable:

  • Set up two or more EC2 On-Demand Instances, enable Auto Scaling, and keep these instances available for the next testing round: This approach may reduce startup time by having running instances, but it's not cost-effective as instances remain on, accruing charges even when not actively used.
  • Implement EC2 Spot Instances to support and automatically scale the application when the next testing period occurs: Spot Instances could help with scaling, but they are not guaranteed to be available when needed and do not address the core issue of slow startup due to memory load times.
  • Provision EC2 On-Demand Instances with Capacity Reservations, then launch further instances as needed in the next testing phase: Capacity Reservations ensure instance availability, but do not improve the actual initialization time of either the instance itself or the application processes.

Tip: For applications that require intensive initialization or long memory preloads, using hibernation in combination with warm pools is highly effective in reducing wait time and costs during on-demand scaling or testing scenarios.

Apply dynamic scaling to automatically modify the size of the Auto Scaling group in response to real-time metric thresholds is the most cost-effective method in scenarios with unpredictable, sudden traffic increases. Dynamic scaling reacts immediately to real-time changes in application demand, automatically adding or removing instances based on metrics such as CPU utilization or request count, helping maintain performance while controlling cost.

Why other options are less effective:

Leverage scheduled scaling to adjust the Auto Scaling group size only changes capacity on predefined schedules. Since the traffic spikes arrive unpredictably, scheduled scaling cannot anticipate nor respond to these random surges.

Utilize predictive scaling to preemptively increase the Auto Scaling group based on historical usage patterns anticipates changes using observed trends. If spikes happen randomly, without a repeatable pattern, predictive scaling may miss or be unable to prepare for these events.

Manually change the Auto Scaling group capacity when required is labor-intensive, slow, and does not scale automatically, leading to possible delays in response and potentially higher costs or reduced application performance.

Tip: For unpredictable or on-demand traffic, always prefer dynamic (sometimes called target tracking or step scaling) policies. Predictive and scheduled scaling are suitable for well-understood and regular patterns, while manual methods are not advisable for production workloads with variable demand.

The best solution is to migrate the PostgreSQL database to Amazon Aurora Serverless v2. This serverless architecture enables the database to automatically and instantly scale capacity up or down based on traffic, charging only for what is actually consumed. This pay-as-you-use model is the most cost-effective for unpredictable and variable workloads, ensuring the application maintains performance during sudden surges without overprovisioning resources.

The other choices are less optimal:

  • Move the PostgreSQL database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL and select a larger instance type. — While Amazon RDS provides managed database services, simply using a larger instance requires paying for the highest resource level at all times—even if the database is underutilized during off-peak periods. This approach lacks elasticity and can result in unnecessary costs.
  • Transfer the workload to Amazon Redshift to better manage increased usage. — Amazon Redshift is designed for data warehousing and analytics workloads, not for OLTP (Online Transactional Processing) typical of ecommerce applications. Migrating a transactional PostgreSQL database to Redshift is inefficient and inappropriate for this use case.
  • Enable autoscaling for the PostgreSQL database running on the EC2 instance to handle fluctuating demand. — EC2 instances hosting PostgreSQL do not offer automatic vertical scaling. While you can horizontally scale application servers, scaling a database running on an EC2 instance is complex, risky, and involves significant downtime. This is neither practical nor cost-effective compared to managed database services designed for elasticity.

Tip: For applications with significant and unpredictable variations in database demand, choosing a scalable, fully managed, and serverless database solution like Aurora Serverless v2 delivers automatic elasticity and cost savings by scaling resources only when needed.

The best solution is to use a Network Load Balancer (NLB) that is publicly reachable on the necessary TCP port. NLBs are engineered to handle millions of requests per second at very low latency and support static IP addresses and custom ports, making them ideal for high-performance, scalable TCP-based workloads.

  • "Use an Application Load Balancer (ALB)..." ALBs only support HTTP and HTTPS protocols, so they're not suitable for TCP applications or nonstandard ports outside these protocols.
  • "Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution listening..." CloudFront is a CDN that only works over HTTP/HTTPS ports and protocols; it cannot distribute arbitrary TCP traffic or listen on custom TCP ports.
  • "Provision a Network Load Balancer (NLB)..." This is correct. NLBs are purposely built for extremely high performance and low latency in TCP (and UDP) traffic, with support for custom ports and static IPs at scale, matching the legacy appliance's capabilities.
  • "Implement an Amazon API Gateway endpoint configured..." API Gateway is designed solely for web protocols (HTTP, HTTPS, WebSocket). It does not accept arbitrary TCP traffic or accommodate custom ports for TCP-level applications.

Tip: For non-HTTP(S), nonstandard port, high-throughput, and low-latency needs, an NLB is almost always the best AWS-native endpoint solution.

Store uploads in S3 Standard and apply a Lifecycle policy to move files to S3 Glacier after 30 days is not suitable because S3 Glacier is optimized for archival rather than frequent or instant access; retrievals take minutes to hours, which doesn't meet availability requirements.

S3 Intelligent-Tiering is best when access patterns are unpredictable, but in this scenario, the pattern after 30 days is predictable.

Tip: Lifecycle policies automate cost optimization. Pick S3 Standard-IA for data accessed less but still requiring high durability and immediate access. Avoid S3 Glacier or S3 One Zone-IA if instant availability and high durability across AZs are mandatory.

The recommended solution is to Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for data ingestion and process the streams through AWS Lambda functions. Kinesis Data Streams acts as a buffer layer to absorb large, bursty incoming data, providing near real-time processing while decoupling the producer (third-party vendor) from the consumer (processing logic). AWS Lambda automatically scales in response to incoming stream records, ensuring compute resources match the workload without manual intervention or risking capacity overruns.   • Deploy the application as a container using Amazon ECS with the EC2 launch type, and utilize an Auto Scaling group: Containerization can improve deployment and management, but if scaling is still EC2-based and not rapid or granular enough, sudden spikes may still result in errors. Provisioning new EC2 instances takes time, leading to periods where requests might still fail.
  • Leverage Amazon SNS to receive the incoming data, and place the EC2 instances within an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer: SNS is designed for messaging/notifications rather than high-throughput ingestion and real-time streaming. Tip: For REST APIs with uneven or unpredictable data inflow, using purpose-built, scalable ingestion mechanisms like Kinesis combined with serverless compute ensures efficient buffering, elasticity, and minimized error rates.

Implement a service control policy (SCP) that blocks CloudTrail modifications and apply it to all developer accounts. is the correct approach. SCPs provide organization-wide guardrails at the AWS Organizations level, and they apply equally to all users and roles—including the root user—within those accounts. This prevents anyone, even root, from making unauthorized changes to CloudTrail, thus enforcing the company's required security posture.

The other options are less effective or technically invalid:

  • Define a service-linked role for CloudTrail with a policy permitting alterations only from a specific ARN belonging to the management account. — Service-linked roles can't be used to restrict root access to CloudTrail configuration, nor do ARN conditions prevent root from making changes.
  • Generate a policy in IAM that denies changes to CloudTrail and apply it directly to the root user. — IAM policies cannot be directly attached to the AWS root user. Only SCPs can restrict root's actions at the account level within an organization.
  • Within each developer's account, establish a new CloudTrail trail using the organizational trails feature. — While this helps with centralized logging, it does not prevent trail modifications by account administrators or root users unless further controls like SCPs are in place.

Tip: Use SCPs for security requirements that must override root and administrator permissions in AWS Organizations. Remember that SCPs set the maximum permissions available in an account—they do not grant permissions but rather restrict them.

The best solution is to deploy a new S3 bucket in the us-east-1 Region, and set up S3 Cross-Region Replication to automatically replicate objects from your original bucket. Cross-Region Replication (CRR) is purpose-built for scenarios like this, providing continuous replication with almost no operational management required after setup. It ensures new uploads to the source bucket are seamlessly copied to the destination bucket in another region.

Let's look at why the other options are less suitable:

  • Configure CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) on the current S3 bucket and set us-east-1 as an allowed origin to enable cross-region copies. — CORS policies do not control or automate cross-region data replication. They are meant for browser-based access control and won't accomplish automatic copying of objects to another region.
  • Add a new S3 bucket in us-east-1 covering multiple Availability Zones, and implement a Lifecycle rule to move images into it. — S3 Lifecycle rules are used to transition objects between storage classes or delete them, but they don't support moving or copying objects between different buckets, especially across regions.
  • Provision a new bucket in us-east-1 and create S3 event notifications for new or modified files to trigger a Lambda function, which copies images to the new bucket. — While this can achieve the goal, it requires ongoing management and introduces additional components (Lambda, IAM permissions, monitoring) that increase complexity and operational effort compared to native S3 Cross-Region Replication.

Tip: Always consider native AWS features (like CRR) as a first choice for requirements such as cross-region replication, as they are designed to be low-maintenance and scalable.

The most effective solution is to Turn off session stickiness (session affinity) on the Application Load Balancer. Enabling session stickiness causes the ALB to route requests from the same client to the same EC2 instance, which can result in one instance receiving the majority of the traffic and increasing latency on that host.

Let's review the other options:

  • Switch to a Network Load Balancer instead of using the existing Application Load Balancer: A Network Load Balancer is typically used for TCP traffic or ultra-low latency workloads. It does not support features like path-based routing, and would not resolve the underlying traffic imbalance caused by stickiness.
  • Change the ALB's target group health check interval: Modifying how frequently health checks occur will not address one instance receiving a disproportionate amount of requests; the issue is traffic distribution, not health checks.
  • Add more EC2 instances to every Availability Zone: Scaling out can improve overall capacity, but if stickiness remains enabled, some instances will still receive more requests, and imbalanced traffic distribution may persist.

Tip: Session stickiness is useful if session data is stored locally on an instance. However, for stateless applications or when you want even traffic distribution, it is best to disable this feature.

To give an AWS Lambda function adequate permissions to decrypt S3 files encrypted with AWS KMS, the following two solutions are sufficient:

  • Provide the decrypt privilege to the Lambda execution IAM role by modifying the KMS key policy. This ensures that the Lambda function’s role has the correct permissions to use the key for decryption; this is achieved by referencing the role in the key policy directly.
  • Create a dedicated IAM role with the kms:decrypt right and set it as the execution role for the Lambda function. By assigning a purpose-built role with the necessary permissions when configuring Lambda, you directly empower the function to decrypt KMS-protected data.

Why are the other options not correct?

  • Attach the kms:decrypt permission to the Lambda function’s resource policy. Lambda does not support resource-based policies for granting KMS permissions this way. KMS key policies and IAM roles are the correct approval mechanisms.
  • Update the KMS key policy to grant decrypt capability specifically to the Lambda resource policy. Lambda’s resource policy is not involved in granting KMS access; permissions must be given via the key policy or the function's IAM execution role.
  • Draft a new IAM policy permitting kms:decrypt and link it directly to the Lambda function. You cannot directly attach an IAM policy to a Lambda function itself; permissions must be included in the execution role assigned to the function.

Tip: Always grant the minimum set of permissions needed (principle of least privilege), and use key policies to tightly scope access.

For this scenario, the transient EMR cluster with On-Demand Instances for the primary and core nodes, and Spot Instances for the task nodes is the ideal configuration. This approach is cost-effective and maintains data durability throughout the processing window.

  • Provision a persistent cluster in which just the primary node is On-Demand, and the core nodes and task nodes are on Spot Instances: Similar to the previous option, this doesn't guarantee the safety of data stored across core nodes since they are relying on non-persistent (Spot) resources, increasing the risk of data loss.

The most effective way to guarantee the application can handle peak loads immediately is to use a scheduled scaling policy that increases the Auto Scaling group size in advance of anticipated high traffic periods. This makes sure enough EC2 instances are running before user requests surge, thus avoiding the performance lag users report at the start of peak hours.

This is correct. Scheduled scaling proactively launches instances before high-demand periods, ensuring the application performs optimally from the very start of peak hours.

Option: Set up a policy to dynamically increase the Auto Scaling group capacity based on CPU usage spikes.
This is incorrect because dynamic scaling based on CPU (or any reactive metric) causes new instances to launch only after high demand is detected, so it can't prevent the initial slowdowns at the beginning of peak time.

Option: Deploy an Application Load Balancer to direct incoming requests more efficiently to EC2 instances.
This is not the best fit, as a load balancer improves distribution of traffic, but does not solve the core issue: there simply aren't enough instances ready at the start of peak load.

Option: Configure a scaling policy so that Auto Scaling responds to memory utilization metrics to launch more instances.
This (also a reactive policy) faces the same challenge as CPU-based scaling: it only adds capacity after user experience has already started to degrade.

Tip: If you can predict demand patterns, define a scheduled action in Auto Scaling to provision resources proactively, not reactively.

Create a VPC endpoint for Amazon RDS for MySQL. Update the security group of the RDS instance to only allow traffic from subnets in which the ECS tasks run. Also, create a VPC endpoint for S3, and configure the S3 bucket policy to restrict access solely through this S3 VPC endpoint. This solution leverages VPC endpoints to keep all traffic within the AWS network, restricting access to both the S3 bucket and the RDS database only to the resources within the specified VPC. By setting the RDS security group to accept traffic only from ECS subnets, and tying the S3 bucket access to the S3 VPC endpoint, external access is prevented, and only the ECS cluster will have permitted access. This meets the requirement to limit connectivity to the ECS cluster alone.

The other choices contain flaws or are incomplete:

  • Set up a customer managed AWS KMS key...Make sure the ECS task execution role is granted encrypt and decrypt permissions in the KMS key policy. While encryption is critical for protecting data at rest and proper key policies are important, this option does not restrict network access to the resources. Encryption alone does not limit who or what can connect to the S3 bucket or RDS database, so other workloads could potentially connect if not blocked by networking controls.
  • Create a bucket policy for S3 that limits access to the ECS tasks' execution role... Restricting the S3 bucket via a bucket policy is a good measure, as is locking down the RDS security group by subnet. However, without an S3 VPC endpoint, S3 can still be accessed from outside the VPC, potentially allowing other AWS identities to gain access. VPC endpoints guarantee that all access stays within the private network.
  • Use an AWS managed KMS key to encrypt both the S3 bucket and RDS for MySQL, and update the S3 bucket policy to include the ECS task execution role as a user. This option, similar to the first, implements encryption and restricts S3 through the policy, but it fails to limit access to RDS and doesn't confine access within the VPC network. To address the need for automatic 30-day retention and subsequent deletion of S3 backup objects, the best approach is a combination of the following:

  • Enable Object Locking on the S3 bucket. This allows you to enforce retention periods and prevent objects from being deleted or modified within the stipulated time, providing immutability for 30 days.
  • Set a default object retention period of 30 days. With Object Lock enabled, you can specify a default retention period for new objects, ensuring all backups are kept for exactly 30 days.
  • Create an S3 Lifecycle rule to delete objects after 30 days. This automates the removal of objects once the 30-day retention period ends, fulfilling the requirement for automatic deletion.

Why not the other choices?

  • Activate object versioning for the S3 bucket. While versioning helps track object changes and deletions, it does not enforce object retention or automate deletions, and alone does not provide immutability or timed deletion.
  • Set an S3 Lifecycle policy to retain backups for 30 days. Although lifecycle policies can delete objects, they do not prevent deletions before 30 days unless combined with Object Lock; retention enforcement is the critical missing component here.
  • Configure the backup product to add a 30-day retention tag to objects. Adding tags represents metadata only; it does not enforce retention or automate deletion. AWS S3 does not automatically act on these tags without a corresponding lifecycle rule, and it does not ensure the objects are protected.

Tip: When your retention policies require regulatory protection (WORM), always use S3 Object Lock, and combine it with lifecycle policies for automatic expiration. Versioning is important for preservation of old versions but is not a substitute for retention enforcement.

Tip: Use AWS Local Zones whenever you need to run latency-sensitive or regulated workloads close to large population centers or specific geographic locations that cannot be hosted in the parent AWS Region.

  • Deploy an Application Load Balancer, enabling session stickiness (affinity) to an Aurora database used for catalog access: Sticky sessions help route a user's requests to the same backend, but if the backend fails or users disconnect and reconnect, session data may be lost. Sticky sessions alone do not provide persistence for cart data across failures or disconnections.
  • Provision an EC2 instance utilizing Elastic Block Store (EBS) volumes for catalog and cart data, and configure scheduled EBS snapshots: While EBS snapshots protect data, this approach lacks the scalability and low latency provided by managed services like ElastiCache. High availability and instant session retrieval are harder to guarantee, especially during instance or network failures.

Tip: For transient, high-speed, and highly available session or shopping cart data, managed in-memory stores like Redis are the industry standard. Consider DynamoDB for permanent records, but in-memory caches like ElastiCache for session and cart data greatly improve performance and reliability.

The correct answer is to Set up an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB) in a public subnet and register the EC2 instance with the ALB’s target group. Make sure the website’s DNS record points to the ALB.

Here's why: Instances launched in private subnets do not have public IP addresses, so they can't accept requests directly from the internet. The standard AWS architecture for exposing resources in a private subnet to the internet is to use an internet-facing ALB (which exists in a public subnet). The ALB can receive internet traffic on behalf of the web server, then forward traffic to EC2 instances running in private subnets.

  • Deploy a NAT gateway in a private subnet, update the private subnet’s route table to point to this gateway, and associate a public Elastic IP address with the NAT gateway. — This is incorrect because a NAT gateway enables outbound internet access for private instances, but it cannot be used to receive inbound traffic from the internet. NAT gateways are not designed to handle or forward unsolicited inbound connections.
  • Adjust the security group of the EC2 instance to allow inbound HTTP (port 80) and HTTPS (port 443) access, and direct the website's DNS record to the instance’s public IP address. — This doesn't work because an instance in a private subnet does not have a public IP. Even with the correct security group rules, internet clients cannot reach it directly.
  • Place the EC2 instance inside an Auto Scaling group in a private subnet, and modify the DNS name for the website to direct traffic to the Auto Scaling group’s identifier. — DNS records cannot resolve to an Auto Scaling group itself, and Auto Scaling groups do not provide an external endpoint. This solution does not make the web servers accessible from the internet.

Tip: In scenarios where private subnets must be maintained for security, pairing them with an ALB is a best practice for exposing internal services securely. Always remember: inbound internet access via NAT Gateway is not possible.

Lastly, Configure the Application Load Balancer to use the round robin algorithm, utilizing RequestCount and TargetResponseTime CloudWatch metrics is incorrect because round robin ignores instance load and therefore does not meet the requirement to avoid sending requests to already overloaded instances.

Tip: Always pair request metrics with relevant response time metrics for effective load balancing decisions—especially when response times vary between targets.

To guarantee that your application retrieves the latest data from DynamoDB, you should use Enable strongly consistent read requests for the DynamoDB table. DynamoDB offers two read consistency models: eventually consistent (the default) and strongly consistent. Eventually consistent reads may return slightly stale data due to the distributed nature of DynamoDB, especially in high-write environments or under replication lag. If your application requires up-to-date, real-time data for every query, strongly consistent reads are essential, even though they might reduce throughput or increase latency slightly.

Why the other options are not suitable:

  • Integrate a global secondary index (GSI) to the table. - Adding a GSI is generally used to enable alternative query patterns, not to address data freshness. GSIs themselves also follow the same consistency models and are subject to replication delay, which does not solve the issue of reading outdated data.
  • Add additional read replicas to the DynamoDB table. - DynamoDB doesn't have traditional read replicas as in RDS; scaling reads is handled differently, and this approach would not fix stale data visibility.
  • Switch to eventually consistent reads for all queries. - This option would potentially increase the occurrence of outdated data retrieval because eventually consistent reads do not guarantee the most recent updates.

Tip: Use strongly consistent reads only when necessary, as they may impact performance and cost. For most workloads where slight staleness is acceptable, eventually consistent reads are sufficient.

The most effective solution is to send incoming score changes to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, process each update using AWS Lambda, and store the results in Amazon DynamoDB. This combination allows for:

  • Order Preservation: Kinesis Data Streams processes data in shards, ensuring events are handled in the order they arrive per shard.
  • High Availability and Scalability: Both Kinesis and DynamoDB are fully managed and support high concurrency while keeping operational overhead low. DynamoDB offers built-in high availability.
  • Minimized Management: AWS Lambda and DynamoDB are serverless and fully managed services, which means minimal effort is needed to maintain infrastructure.

Why are the other choices less suitable?

  • Route score updates to an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream, use a group of Auto Scaling EC2 instances to process the updates, and store the processed data in Amazon Redshift: Running EC2 fleets increases management tasks, and Amazon Redshift is intended for analytics, not transactional or quick leaderboard updates.
  • Deliver score notifications to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) topic, subscribe a Lambda function for processing, and keep the results in a SQL database hosted on Amazon EC2: SNS does not preserve the order of messages, and maintaining a SQL database on EC2 requires scaling and high availability management you want to avoid.
  • Transmit score data via Amazon SQS, have a set of Auto Scaling EC2 instances process the queued messages, and store final scores in a Multi-AZ Amazon RDS instance: SQS provides at-least-once and best-effort ordering (not strict order), and managing EC2 and RDS clusters increases management overhead.

Tip: For streaming ingestion where order and minimal ops overhead are necessary, AWS Kinesis with Lambda and DynamoDB is a classic architectural pattern.

The Amazon EventBridge solution is the best option for deploying this architecture while minimizing operational overhead. EventBridge allows you to route incoming messages to multiple Lambda functions and offers native support for message filtering using its rules engine, so each function only receives specific messages it needs. No manual polling or maintenance of batch-processing code is required, keeping operations simple and scalable.

Here's why the other choices are not optimal:

  • Direct API Gateway REST API calls to multiple Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) queues, and configure each Lambda function to poll its respective queue. — SQS does not support content-based message filtering by default, and each Lambda must continually poll its queue or be configured with triggers. Managing multiple queues and polling logic increases operational complexity.
  • Forward API Gateway REST API messages to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) topic, subscribe Amazon SQS queues to the topic, and have the Lambda functions poll from these queues. — While SNS supports basic filtering on message attributes, using SQS in combination to buffer messages adds extra layers of management, as well as the need for polling and queue handling.
  • Connect the API Gateway REST API to Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK), and arrange for MSK to deliver messages to the Lambda functions. — Although MSK can route messages, it's an over-engineered solution for this requirement, incurs greater setup and maintenance responsibilities, and does not natively offer simple message filtering for Lambda triggers compared to EventBridge.

Pro Tip: Use Amazon EventBridge when you need advanced event routing and payload-based filtering with minimal infrastructure upkeep. It is specifically designed for event-driven, serverless workloads and integrates tightly with Lambda.

AWS AppConfig is specifically designed for managing and deploying application configurations centrally and securely, reducing risk and operational effort. AWS Secrets Manager is built for securely storing and retrieving sensitive information such as database credentials, offering automatic rotation, audit logs, and fine-grained access control to further minimize administrative overhead.

The other options are less optimal for the following reasons:

  • Implement AWS Lambda to store application settings, and utilize AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store for credentials management. Lambda is a compute service, not a configuration store. Parameter Store can help with credentials, but using Lambda for configuration is inappropriate and introduces unnecessary complexity.
  • Encrypt application configuration, keep it in an S3 bucket, and place credentials in a separate S3 object for applications to fetch. This approach places the burden of encryption, decryption, and secure access management on the team, increasing administrative overhead and potentially leading to misconfigurations.
  • Apply AWS AppConfig for storing configuration data, and use Amazon RDS itself for handling and retrieving credentials. RDS is not meant to be a credential store; using the database to keep secrets contradicts security best practices and adds unneeded complexity.

Tip: Use purpose-built services for configuration and secrets management to benefit from integrated security, automation, and monitoring capabilities. This also aids compliance and improves application maintainability.

The correct option is Retrieve the AWS-issued root certificates and use them to establish secure, encrypted (SSL/TLS) connections to the RDS instance. This ensures that all communication between your applications and the Amazon RDS MySQL database is encrypted in transit, satisfying the security requirements for protecting data as it travels over the network.

Let's break down the other options:

  • Enable IAM authentication for the RDS database. IAM authentication is used for credential management and user access but does not encrypt data in transit. It is a separate security control.
  • Provide custom, self-generated SSL certificates and use them to connect to the RDS MySQL instance. Amazon RDS does not support using self-signed SSL certificates for database connections. Clients must use the AWS-provided certificates for SSL/TLS connections.
  • Create a backup snapshot of the RDS database and restore it to a new instance with data encryption enabled. This action only affects encryption at rest and has no impact on securing data in transit. Since encryption at rest is already enabled, this does not address the question's requirement.

Tip: Always use the database engine’s native support for encrypted connections and download root CA certificates from AWS to establish proper trust. Encryption at rest and in transit are separate controls, and both must be explicitly configured to fully secure your database solution.
